<script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w18">{"year":2,"week":18,"id":"y2w18","title":"Surface Area: Nets, Formulas and SI and Imperial Units","subtitle":"Surface area and why it matters; square units in the SI system (m², cm²) and the imperial system (ft², in²) and converting between them; nets of prisms, pyramids, cylinders and cones; formulas for the surface area of cubes, cuboids, prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres; finding a missing dimension; composite solids; and checking answers.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":7,"name":"Surface Areas and Volumes","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":18,"to":20},"outcomes":["Explain surface area and use nets to find the surface area of prisms and pyramids.","Convert areas between m² and cm², ft² and in², and between SI and imperial units.","Use formulas for the surface area of cylinders, cones and spheres, finding a slant height by Pythagoras.","Work backwards from a surface area to a missing length.","Solve real problems such as painting and packaging, and verify the answers."],"keywords":["surface area","net","face","lateral surface","curved surface","total surface area","square metre","square centimetre","square foot","square inch","SI unit","imperial unit","conversion factor","prism","pyramid","cylinder","cone","slant height","sphere","hemisphere","composite solid"],"notes":[{"title":"What is surface area?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **surface area** of a solid is the total area of all its faces and curved surfaces. If you open a box out flat, you get its **net**; the surface area is the area of the net."},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Why it matters","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Surface area tells a painter how much paint to buy, a packaging company how much card a box needs, a tailor how much cloth covers a cushion, and a builder how many roofing sheets a roof needs."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Units of area","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w18-units","caption":"Square units in the SI and imperial systems."},{"k":"table","head":["Conversion","Rule"],"rows":[["m² to cm²","$\\times10\\,000$ (because $1\\text{ m}=100\\text{ cm}$ and $100^2=10\\,000$)"],["ft² to in²","$\\times144$ (because $1\\text{ ft}=12\\text{ in}$ and $12^2=144$)"],["m² to ft²","$\\times10.7639$"],["ft² to m²","$\\times0.092903$ (or $\\div10.7639$)"],["in² to cm²","$\\times6.4516$ (because $1\\text{ in}=2.54\\text{ cm}$ and $2.54^2=6.4516$)"],["cm² to in²","$\\div6.4516$ (or $\\times0.155$)"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Square the length factor","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To convert **areas**, square the factor for lengths. Since $1\\text{ m}=100\\text{ cm}$, $1\\text{ m}^2$ is $100^2=10\\,000\\text{ cm}^2$, not 100."}]}],"figs":["w18-units"]},{"title":"Nets and surface area","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w18-net","caption":"A cuboid and its net."},{"k":"p","text":"For any **prism** (a solid with the same cross-section all along its length):"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{SA}=2A+P\\times L"},{"k":"p","text":"where $A$ is the area of the cross-section, $P$ its perimeter and $L$ the length of the prism."},{"k":"p","text":"For a **pyramid**: surface area $=$ area of the base $+$ the areas of the triangular faces."}],"figs":["w18-net"]},{"title":"Formulas","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Solid","Total surface area"],"rows":[["cube, edge $a$","$6a^2$"],["cuboid $l\\times w\\times h$","$2(lw+wh+lh)$"],["cylinder, radius $r$, height $h$","$2\\pi r^2+2\\pi rh=2\\pi r(r+h)$"],["cone, radius $r$, slant height $l$","$\\pi r^2+\\pi rl=\\pi r(r+l)$"],["sphere, radius $r$","$4\\pi r^2$"],["solid hemisphere","$2\\pi r^2+\\pi r^2=3\\pi r^2$"]]},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-cylcone","caption":"Nets of a cylinder and a cone."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Slant height","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The slant height $l$ of a cone is not its vertical height $h$. They are linked by Pythagoras: $\\ l=\\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$. The same idea gives the slant height of a pyramid's faces."}]}],"figs":["w18-cylcone"]},{"title":"Checking your answer","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Units:** areas must be in **square** units.","**Estimate:** round the dimensions and check the size of the answer.","**Reverse:** substitute your answer back, for example check that a side of 4 gives $6\\times4^2=96$."]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Converting area units","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Convert (a) 2 m² to cm² (b) 15 000 cm² to m² (c) 3 ft² to in² (d) 288 in² to ft²."}],"steps":["(a) $2\\times10\\,000=20\\,000$ cm².","(b) $15\\,000\\div10\\,000=1.5$ m².","(c) $3\\times144=432$ in².","(d) $288\\div144=2$ ft²."],"answer":"(a) 20 000 cm² (b) 1.5 m² (c) 432 in² (d) 2 ft²","figs":[]},{"title":"Between SI and imperial","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Convert (a) 8 m² to ft² (b) 50 ft² to m² (c) 150 cm² to in² (d) 300 in² to cm²."}],"steps":["(a) $8\\times10.7639\\approx86.11$ ft².","(b) $50\\div10.7639\\approx4.645$ m².","(c) $150\\div6.4516\\approx23.25$ in².","(d) $300\\times6.4516=1935.48$ cm²."],"answer":"(a) 86.11 ft² (b) 4.645 m² (c) 23.25 in² (d) 1935.48 cm²","figs":[]},{"title":"A cuboid from its net","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the surface area of a cuboid 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm high."}],"steps":["The net has three pairs of equal faces (see the figure in the notes).","Areas: $8\\times5=40$, $\\ 8\\times3=24$, $\\ 5\\times3=15$ cm².","Surface area $=2(40+24+15)=158$ cm².","Check with the formula: $2(lw+wh+lh)=2(40+15+24)=158$ ✓."],"answer":"158 cm²","figs":[]},{"title":"A triangular prism","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A prism has equilateral triangular ends of side 5 m and height 4.3 m, and is 7 m long. Find its surface area."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-tri","caption":"The net of the triangular prism."}],"steps":["Two triangles: $2\\times\\tfrac12\\times5\\times4.3=21.5$ m².","Three rectangles, each $5\\times7=35$ m²: total 105 m².","Surface area $=21.5+105=126.5$ m².","Prism formula check: $2(10.75)+(5+5+5)\\times7=21.5+105$ ✓."],"answer":"126.5 m²","figs":["w18-tri"]},{"title":"Cylinder and cone","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Find the total surface area of a cylinder of radius 3.5 cm and height 6 cm $\\left(\\pi=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\right)$. (b) An ice-cream cone has radius 4 in and slant height 7 in. Find its total surface area. (c) A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its total surface area."}],"steps":["(a) $2\\pi r(r+h)=2\\times\\tfrac{22}{7}\\times3.5\\times9.5=209$ cm².","(b) $\\pi r(r+l)=\\pi\\times4\\times11=44\\pi\\approx138.2$ in².","(c) Slant height $l=\\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$ cm, so the surface area is $\\pi\\times5\\times(5+13)=90\\pi\\approx282.7$ cm²."],"answer":"(a) 209 cm² (b) about 138.2 in² (c) about 282.7 cm²","figs":[]},{"title":"A square-based pyramid","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A pyramid has a square base of side 6 cm and the slant height of each triangular face is 5 cm. Find its surface area."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-pyramid","caption":"A square-based pyramid and its net."}],"steps":["Base: $6\\times6=36$ cm².","Each triangle: $\\tfrac12\\times6\\times5=15$ cm², and there are 4 of them: 60 cm².","Surface area $=36+60=96$ cm²."],"answer":"96 cm²","figs":["w18-pyramid"]},{"title":"Working backwards","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A cube has surface area 96 cm². Find the length of its edge. (b) A sphere has surface area 154 cm². Find its radius $\\left(\\pi=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\right)$."}],"steps":["(a) $6a^2=96$, so $a^2=16$ and $a=4$ cm.","(b) $4\\pi r^2=154$, so $r^2=\\dfrac{154}{4\\times\\tfrac{22}{7}}=\\dfrac{154\\times7}{88}=12.25$.","$r=\\sqrt{12.25}=3.5$ cm."],"answer":"(a) 4 cm (b) 3.5 cm","figs":[]},{"title":"Painting a room","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A room is 12 ft long, 10 ft wide and 8 ft high. The four walls and the ceiling are to be painted, but not the door (3 ft by 7 ft) or the window (4 ft by 3 ft). One litre of paint covers 10 m² and costs GH₵85. How much paint is needed, and what does it cost if paint is sold in whole litres?"}],"steps":["Walls: $2(12+10)\\times8=352$ ft². Ceiling: $12\\times10=120$ ft². Total 472 ft².","Subtract the door (21 ft²) and window (12 ft²): $472-33=439$ ft².","In m²: $439\\times0.092903\\approx40.8$ m².","Paint $=\\dfrac{40.8}{10}=4.08$ L, so buy 5 litres: cost $5\\times85=$ GH₵425.","Check: $440\\text{ ft}^2\\div10.76\\approx41$ m² ✓."],"answer":"5 litres, GH₵425","figs":[]},{"title":"A composite solid","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A grain silo is a cylinder of radius 3 m and height 10 m with a hemispherical roof. Find the area of metal sheet needed for the curved wall and the roof (no base)."}],"steps":["Curved wall of the cylinder: $2\\pi rh=2\\pi\\times3\\times10=60\\pi$ m².","Hemispherical roof (curved surface only): $2\\pi r^2=2\\pi\\times9=18\\pi$ m².","Total $=78\\pi\\approx245.0$ m²."],"answer":"about 245 m²","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Surface area","items":["Surface area $=$ total area of all faces $=$ area of the net.","1 m² $=10\\,000$ cm²; 1 ft² $=144$ in²; 1 m² $\\approx10.7639$ ft²; 1 in² $=6.4516$ cm².","Prism: $2\\times$ cross-section $+$ perimeter $\\times$ length.","Cylinder $2\\pi r(r+h)$; cone $\\pi r(r+l)$ with $l=\\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$; sphere $4\\pi r^2$.","Check units (square), estimate, and substitute back."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"3 m² in cm² is","options":["30 000 cm²","300 cm²","3000 cm²","0.03 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$3\\times10\\,000$."},{"q":"5 ft² in in² is","options":["720 in²","60 in²","144 in²","600 in²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$5\\times144$."},{"q":"1 in $=2.54$ cm, so 1 in² is","options":["6.4516 cm²","2.54 cm²","5.08 cm²","0.155 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$2.54^2$."},{"q":"The surface area of a cube of edge 5 cm is","options":["150 cm²","125 cm²","25 cm²","100 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$6\\times25$."},{"q":"The surface area of a cuboid 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm is","options":["52 cm²","24 cm²","26 cm²","48 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$2(12+6+8)$."},{"q":"The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius 2 cm and height 5 cm is","options":["$20\\pi$ cm²","$28\\pi$ cm²","$10\\pi$ cm²","$40\\pi$ cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$2\\pi rh$."},{"q":"A cone has radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Its slant height is","options":["5 cm","7 cm","1 cm","12 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\sqrt{9+16}$."},{"q":"The surface area of a sphere of radius 3 cm is","options":["$36\\pi$ cm²","$12\\pi$ cm²","$9\\pi$ cm²","$108\\pi$ cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$4\\pi\\times9$."},{"q":"A cube has surface area 54 cm². Its edge is","options":["3 cm","9 cm","6 cm","2 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$a^2=9$."},{"q":"Which is the correct unit for a surface area?","options":["m²","m","m³","litres"],"correct":0,"explain":"Areas are measured in square units."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Convert (a) 12 m² to ft² (b) 80 ft² to m².","a":"(a) about 129.17 ft² (b) about 7.43 m²"},{"q":"Convert (a) 250 cm² to in² (b) 450 in² to cm².","a":"(a) about 38.75 in² (b) 2903.22 cm²"},{"q":"Find the surface area of a cube with edge 4 units.","a":"96 square units"},{"q":"Find the surface area of a cuboid 5 by 3 by 2 units.","a":"$2(15+6+10)=62$ square units"},{"q":"Find the total surface area of a cone with radius 4 and slant height 7.","a":"$44\\pi\\approx138.2$"},{"q":"Find the total surface area of a cylinder with radius 5 and height 10.","a":"$150\\pi\\approx471.2$"},{"q":"Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 6.","a":"$144\\pi\\approx452.4$"},{"q":"Find the surface area of a square prism with base edge 3 and height 8.","a":"$2(9)+4(3)(8)=114$"},{"q":"A cube has surface area 150 square units. Find its edge.","a":"5 units"},{"q":"A cuboid has surface area 94 square units and a base 3 by 4. Find its height.","a":"$24+14h=94$: $h=5$"},{"q":"A cylinder has surface area 282.6 and radius 3 ($\\pi=3.14$). Find its height.","a":"$18.84(3+h)=282.6$: $h=12$"},{"q":"Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm $\\left(\\pi=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\right)$.","a":"$3\\pi r^2=462$ cm²"}],"theory":[{"q":"Use the net of a cone to show that its curved surface area is $\\pi rl$.","steps":["The curved surface opens out into a **sector** of a circle of radius $l$ (the slant height). The arc of the sector wraps round the base, so its length is the base circumference $2\\pi r$.","A full circle of radius $l$ has circumference $2\\pi l$ and area $\\pi l^2$. The sector is the fraction $\\dfrac{2\\pi r}{2\\pi l}=\\dfrac rl$ of that circle, so its area is $\\frac rl\\times\\pi l^2=\\pi rl.$","Adding the circular base gives the total surface area $\\pi rl+\\pi r^2=\\pi r(r+l)$."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Show that the surface area of a regular hexagonal prism with base edge $a$ and length $h$ is $6ah+3\\sqrt3\\,a^2$. Find it when $a=4$ cm and $h=10$ cm.","steps":["A regular hexagon of side $a$ is made of 6 equilateral triangles, each of area $\\tfrac{\\sqrt3}{4}a^2$, so the hexagon's area is $\\tfrac{3\\sqrt3}{2}a^2$. Two ends give $3\\sqrt3\\,a^2$.","The six rectangular sides are each $a\\times h$, giving $6ah$. So the total is $6ah+3\\sqrt3\\,a^2$.","For $a=4$, $h=10$: $\\ 240+48\\sqrt3\\approx240+83.1=323.1$ cm²."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A company packs a ball of radius 5 cm in a cube-shaped box that just fits around it. (a) Find the surface area of the ball and of the box. (b) What percentage of the box's surface area is the ball's surface area?","steps":["(a) Ball: $4\\pi\\times5^2=100\\pi\\approx314.2$ cm². The box has edge $2r=10$ cm, so its surface area is $6\\times100=600$ cm².","(b) $\\dfrac{100\\pi}{600}\\times100\\%=\\dfrac{\\pi}{6}\\times100\\%\\approx52.4\\%$. The ratio does not depend on the size of the ball."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Two similar cylinders have heights 6 cm and 9 cm. The smaller has total surface area 120 cm². Find the surface area of the larger, and explain your method.","steps":["For similar solids every length is multiplied by the same scale factor $k=\\dfrac{9}{6}=1.5$.","Area is length $\\times$ length, so every area is multiplied by $k^2=2.25$.","Larger surface area $=120\\times2.25=270$ cm²."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A tent is a triangular prism 3 m long. Its triangular ends have base 2.4 m and two sloping sides of 2 m. The ground sheet (the base) is included. Find the area of canvas needed, and convert it to square feet.","steps":["Height of each triangle: $\\sqrt{2^2-1.2^2}=\\sqrt{2.56}=1.6$ m, so each end has area $\\tfrac12\\times2.4\\times1.6=1.92$ m².","Rectangles: two sloping sides $2\\times3=6$ m² each and the ground sheet $2.4\\times3=7.2$ m².","Total $=2(1.92)+2(6)+7.2=23.04$ m², about $23.04\\times10.7639\\approx248.0$ ft²."],"answer":"","model":null}],"checklist":["I can explain surface area and draw nets of common solids.","I can convert areas between m², cm², ft² and in².","I can find the surface area of prisms <script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w19">{"year":2,"week":19,"id":"y2w19","title":"Volume and Capacity: SI and Imperial Units","subtitle":"Volume and capacity and the difference between them; cubic units, litres and millilitres; cubic feet, cubic inches, gallons, quarts, pints and fluid ounces, and converting between SI and imperial units; volumes of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres; missing dimensions; composite solids; and recasting one solid into another.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":7,"name":"Surface Areas and Volumes","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":18,"to":20},"outcomes":["Explain the difference between volume and capacity and choose suitable units.","Convert volumes and capacities between cm³, m³, mL and L, and between SI and imperial units.","Use formulas for the volume of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres.","Find a missing dimension from a given volume.","Find the volume of composite solids and of a solid recast into another shape."],"keywords":["volume","capacity","cubic centimetre","cubic metre","litre","millilitre","cubic foot","cubic inch","cubic yard","gallon","quart","pint","fluid ounce","conversion factor","prism","cylinder","pyramid","cone","sphere","hemisphere","composite solid","frustum"],"notes":[{"title":"Volume and capacity","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Volume** is the amount of space a solid or substance takes up. **Capacity** is the greatest amount a hollow container can hold. A full bottle of water: the **volume** of the water equals the **capacity** of the bottle; when half full, the volume of water is half the capacity."},{"k":"table","head":["","Volume","Capacity"],"rows":[["meaning","space taken up","amount a container can hold"],["applies to","solid and hollow objects","hollow objects only"],["usual units","cm³, m³, in³, ft³","mL, L, gallons, pints"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"SI units","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w19-litre","caption":"A litre is a 10 cm cube; a thousand of them fill a cubic metre."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"SI volume and capacity","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$1\\text{ cm}^3=1\\text{ mL}$ and $1000\\text{ cm}^3=1\\text{ L}$.","$1\\text{ m}^3=100^3\\text{ cm}^3=1\\,000\\,000\\text{ cm}^3=1000\\text{ L}$.","For volumes, **cube** the length factor: $1\\text{ m}=100\\text{ cm}$, so $1\\text{ m}^3=100^3\\text{ cm}^3$."]}]}],"figs":["w19-litre"]},{"title":"Imperial units","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Unit","Equivalent"],"rows":[["1 cubic foot (ft³)","$12^3=1728$ in³"],["1 cubic yard (yd³)","$3^3=27$ ft³"],["1 US gallon","4 quarts $=8$ pints $=128$ fluid ounces $=231$ in³"],["1 UK (imperial) gallon","about 4.546 L"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Converting between systems","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Conversion","Multiply by"],"rows":[["m³ to ft³","35.3147"],["ft³ to m³","0.0283168"],["litres to US gallons","0.264172"],["US gallons to litres","3.78541"],["in³ to cm³","16.387 ($=2.54^3$)"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Which gallon?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The US gallon (3.785 L) and the UK gallon (4.546 L) are different. Use the one the question states; in this book \"gallon\" means the US gallon unless it says otherwise."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Volume formulas","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w19-solids","caption":"Volume formulas for four solids."},{"k":"table","head":["Solid","Volume"],"rows":[["prism (any constant cross-section $A$, length $l$)","$V=Al$"],["cuboid","$V=lwh$"],["cylinder","$V=\\pi r^2h$"],["pyramid (base area $B$, height $h$)","$V=\\tfrac13Bh$"],["cone","$V=\\tfrac13\\pi r^2h$"],["sphere","$V=\\tfrac43\\pi r^3$"],["hemisphere","$V=\\tfrac23\\pi r^3$"]]},{"k":"p","text":"A cone holds exactly a third of a cylinder with the same base and height; the same is true of a pyramid and a prism."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-third","caption":"Three cones fill a cylinder of the same base and height."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Composite solids and recasting","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Composite solid:** split it into simple solids, find each volume, and add (or subtract a hole).","**Recasting:** when a solid is melted and remoulded, its **volume stays the same**. Set the two volume formulas equal and solve."]}]}],"figs":["w19-solids","w19-third"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Converting volumes and capacities","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Convert (a) 2 m³ to ft³ (b) 3.5 m³ to litres (c) 10 L to US gallons (d) 10 ft³ to m³ (e) 5 US gallons to litres."}],"steps":["(a) $2\\times35.3147\\approx70.63$ ft³.","(b) $3.5\\times1000=3500$ L.","(c) $10\\times0.264172\\approx2.64$ gallons.","(d) $10\\times0.0283168\\approx0.283$ m³.","(e) $5\\times3.78541\\approx18.93$ L."],"answer":"(a) 70.63 ft³ (b) 3500 L (c) 2.64 gal (d) 0.283 m³ (e) 18.93 L","figs":[]},{"title":"A cylinder and its capacity","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A cylindrical tin has radius 5 cm and height 13 cm. Find its volume to 2 decimal places $\\left(\\pi=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\right)$ and its capacity in litres."}],"steps":["$V=\\pi r^2h=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\times25\\times13=\\tfrac{7150}{7}\\approx1021.43$ cm³.","$1000$ cm³ $=1$ L, so the capacity is about 1.02 L."],"answer":"1021.43 cm³, about 1.02 L","figs":[]},{"title":"A sphere","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the volume of a sphere with diameter 9 mm, to 3 significant figures."}],"steps":["Radius $r=9\\div2=4.5$ mm.","$V=\\tfrac43\\pi(4.5)^3=\\tfrac43\\pi\\times91.125=121.5\\pi\\approx381.7$ mm³.","To 3 s.f., $V\\approx382$ mm³."],"answer":"about 382 mm³","figs":[]},{"title":"Missing dimensions","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A cuboid has volume 2016 cm³, length 8 cm and width 14 cm. Find its height."}],"steps":["(a) $8\\times14\\times x=2016$, so $112x=2016$ and $x=18$ cm.","(b) $\\pi r^2(6.4)=160\\pi$, so $r^2=25$ and $r=5$ cm.","(c) $\\tfrac13\\times3600\\times h=66\\,000$, so $1200h=66\\,000$ and $h=55$ cm."],"answer":"(a) 18 cm (b) 5 cm (c) 55 cm","figs":[]},{"title":"A cuboid with a pyramid on top","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The solid is a cuboid 12 cm by 12 cm by 15 cm with a square-based pyramid on top. Its total height is 23 cm. Find its volume."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-composite","caption":"A cuboid topped by a pyramid."}],"steps":["Cuboid: $12\\times12\\times15=2160$ cm³.","Pyramid height $=23-15=8$ cm; volume $=\\tfrac13\\times144\\times8=384$ cm³.","Total $=2160+384=2544$ cm³."],"answer":"2544 cm³","figs":["w19-composite"]},{"title":"A cylinder with a cone on top","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A solid is made of a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 10 cm with a cone of the same radius and height 6 cm on top. Find its volume, and its capacity in litres if it were hollow."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-cylcone","caption":"A cylinder topped by a cone."}],"steps":["Cylinder: $\\pi(4^2)(10)=160\\pi$ cm³.","Cone: $\\tfrac13\\pi(4^2)(6)=32\\pi$ cm³.","Total $=192\\pi\\approx603.2$ cm³, which is about 0.603 L."],"answer":"about 603.2 cm³ (0.603 L)","figs":["w19-cylcone"]},{"title":"How many cups?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A paper cup is a cone of radius 3.5 cm and depth 12 cm. How many full cups can be poured from 2 litres of water $\\left(\\pi=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\right)$?"}],"steps":["Capacity of a cup $=\\tfrac13\\times\\tfrac{22}{7}\\times3.5^2\\times12=154$ cm³.","$2$ L $=2000$ cm³, and $\\dfrac{2000}{154}\\approx12.99$.","So **12** full cups can be poured (the 13th cup would be almost, but not quite, full)."],"answer":"12 cups","figs":[]},{"title":"An imperial aquarium","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An aquarium is 12 in long, 8 in wide and 8 in high. Find its capacity in US gallons and in litres (1 gallon $=231$ in³)."}],"steps":["Volume $=12\\times8\\times8=768$ in³.","In gallons: $\\dfrac{768}{231}\\approx3.32$ gal.","In litres: $3.32\\times3.78541\\approx12.6$ L. (Check: $768\\times16.387\\approx12\\,585$ cm³ $\\approx12.6$ L ✓.)"],"answer":"about 3.32 gallons, 12.6 litres","figs":[]},{"title":"Recasting a solid","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into a cylinder of radius 4 cm. Find the height of the cylinder."}],"steps":["Volume of the sphere $=\\tfrac43\\pi(6^3)=288\\pi$ cm³.","The volume is unchanged: $\\pi(4^2)h=288\\pi$.","$16h=288$, so $h=18$ cm."],"answer":"18 cm","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Volume and capacity","items":["$1\\text{ cm}^3=1\\text{ mL}$; $1000\\text{ cm}^3=1\\text{ L}$; $1\\text{ m}^3=1000\\text{ L}$.","1 ft³ $=1728$ in³; 1 yd³ $=27$ ft³; 1 US gal $=3.785$ L $=231$ in³; 1 m³ $\\approx35.31$ ft³.","Prism $Al$; cylinder $\\pi r^2h$; pyramid $\\tfrac13Bh$; cone $\\tfrac13\\pi r^2h$; sphere $\\tfrac43\\pi r^3$.","Composite solids: add the parts. Recasting: volume is unchanged."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"1 litre is equal to","options":["1000 cm³","100 cm³","1 m³","10 cm³"],"correct":0,"explain":"A litre is a 10 cm cube."},{"q":"2.5 m³ in litres is","options":["2500 L","250 L","25 000 L","0.0025 L"],"correct":0,"explain":"$1\\text{ m}^3=1000$ L."},{"q":"1 ft³ in cubic inches is","options":["1728 in³","144 in³","12 in³","36 in³"],"correct":0,"explain":"$12^3$."},{"q":"The volume of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm is","options":["$90\\pi$ cm³","$30\\pi$ cm³","$60\\pi$ cm³","$900\\pi$ cm³"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\pi\\times9\\times10$."},{"q":"A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height. The cone's volume is","options":["one third of the cylinder's","half of the cylinder's","equal to the cylinder's","three times the cylinder's"],"correct":0,"explain":"$V=\\tfrac13\\pi r^2h$."},{"q":"The volume of a sphere of radius 3 cm is","options":["$36\\pi$ cm³","$12\\pi$ cm³","$27\\pi$ cm³","$108\\pi$ cm³"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac43\\pi\\times27$."},{"q":"A square pyramid has base edge 6 cm and height 5 cm. Its volume is","options":["60 cm³","180 cm³","90 cm³","30 cm³"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac13\\times36\\times5$."},{"q":"4 US gallons is about","options":["15.1 litres","1.06 litres","4 litres","18.2 litres"],"correct":0,"explain":"$4\\times3.785$."},{"q":"A cuboid has volume 120 cm³, length 6 cm and width 5 cm. Its height is","options":["4 cm","20 cm","24 cm","109 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$120\\div30$."},{"q":"When a solid is melted and recast, what stays the same?","options":["its volume","its surface area","its height","its shape"],"correct":0,"explain":"The amount of material does not change."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Convert (a) 4.2 m³ to litres (b) 750 mL to cm³ (c) 0.35 L to mL.","a":"(a) 4200 L (b) 750 cm³ (c) 350 mL"},{"q":"Convert (a) 50 L to US gallons (b) 25 ft³ to m³ (c) 20 US gallons to litres.","a":"(a) 13.21 gal (b) 0.708 m³ (c) 75.71 L"},{"q":"Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm $\\left(\\pi=\\tfrac{22}{7}\\right)$.","a":"1540 cm³"},{"q":"Find the volume of a rectangular-based pyramid with base 10 cm by 6 cm and height 9 cm.","a":"180 cm³"},{"q":"A cuboid has volume 720 mm³, length 8 mm and width 9 mm. Find the missing side.","a":"10 mm"},{"q":"Find the volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm.","a":"$18\\pi\\approx56.5$ cm³"},{"q":"Find the volume of a cone of radius 6 cm and slant height 10 cm.","a":"$h=8$: $96\\pi\\approx301.6$ cm³"},{"q":"A solid is a cube of edge 6 cm with a square-based pyramid of height 4 cm on top. Find its volume.","a":"$216+48=264$ cm³"},{"q":"A cylindrical tank of radius 0.5 m and height 1.2 m is full of water. How many litres does it hold?","a":"$0.3\\pi\\approx0.942$ m³ $\\approx942$ L"},{"q":"How many cubic inches are in a 2-gallon bucket (1 gal $=231$ in³)?","a":"462 in³"}],"theory":[{"q":"Show that $1\\text{ m}^3=1000$ litres and that $1\\text{ ft}^3=1728\\text{ in}^3$. Hence, using $1\\text{ m}\\approx3.2808$ ft, show that $1\\text{ m}^3\\approx35.31\\text{ ft}^3$.","steps":["$1\\text{ m}=100$ cm, so $1\\text{ m}^3=100\\times100\\times100=1\\,000\\,000$ cm³. Since $1\\text{ L}=1000$ cm³, this is $1\\,000\\,000\\div1000=1000$ L.","$1\\text{ ft}=12$ in, so $1\\text{ ft}^3=12^3=1728$ in³.","$1\\text{ m}^3=(3.2808\\text{ ft})^3=3.2808^3\\text{ ft}^3\\approx35.31$ ft³. Lengths convert by the factor, areas by its square, volumes by its cube."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"An ice cream is a cone of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm, filled level and topped with a hemisphere of radius 3 cm. Find the total volume of ice cream.","steps":["Cone: $\\tfrac13\\pi(3^2)(10)=30\\pi$ cm³.","Hemisphere: $\\tfrac23\\pi(3^3)=18\\pi$ cm³.","Total $=48\\pi\\approx150.8$ cm³."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A bucket is a frustum (a cone with its tip cut off). Its top radius is 15 cm, its base radius is 10 cm and its depth is 24 cm. Find its capacity in litres.","steps":["Extend the sides to make a full cone of height $H$. By similar triangles, $\\dfrac{15}{H}=\\dfrac{10}{H-24}$, so $15H-360=10H$ and $H=72$ cm. The small cone removed has height 48 cm. $V=\\tfrac13\\pi(15^2)(72)-\\tfrac13\\pi(10^2)(48)=5400\\pi-1600\\pi=3800\\pi$","$3800\\pi\\approx11\\,938$ cm³, so the bucket holds about **11.9 litres**."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Two similar water jugs have heights 10 cm and 15 cm. The smaller holds 0.8 L. How much does the larger hold? Explain why.","steps":["The scale factor for lengths is $k=\\dfrac{15}{10}=1.5$.","Volume is length $\\times$ length $\\times$ length, so volumes are multiplied by $k^3=3.375$.","The larger jug holds $0.8\\times3.375=2.7$ L."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A lead pipe is a hollow cylinder 2 m long, with outer radius 3 cm and inner radius 2.5 cm. (a) Find the volume of lead. (b) Lead has a density of 11.3 g per cm³. Find the mass of the pipe in kg.","steps":["(a) Length $=200$ cm. Volume $=\\pi(3^2-2.5^2)(200)=\\pi(2.75)(200)=550\\pi\\approx1727.9$ cm³.","(b) Mass $=1727.9\\times11.3\\approx19\\,525$ g, about **19.5 kg**."],"answer":"","model":null}],"checklist":["I can explain the difference between volume and capacity.","I can convert between cm³, m³, mL and L.","I can convert volumes between SI and imperial units.","I can find volumes of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres.","I can find a missing dimension from a volume.","I can find volumes of composite and recast solids."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[1]}],[{"j":4,"notes":false,"exs":[2,3,4,5,6,7,8]}]],"exSec":[3,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],"quizSec":[1,3,2,4,4,4,4,3,4,4],"exerSec":[3,3,4,4,4,4,4,4,0,2],"thSec":[3,4,0,0,0],"sumSec":[0,0,4,4],"chkSec":[0,3,2,4,0,4],"weights":[529.7,679.85,380.1,1362.05,6828.85],"figs":[{"id":"w19-litre","sec":1,"lesson":1,"caption":"A litre is a 10 cm cube; a thousand of them fill a cubic metre."},{"id":"w19-composite","sec":4,"lesson":2,"ex":4,"caption":"A cuboid topped by a pyramid."}]},"next":"Volume and Capacity in the Real World","tm":{"sectionNo":7,"sectionName":"Surface Areas and Volumes","strand":"Geometry Around Us","sub":"Measurement","cs":["Demonstrate conceptual understanding of the measurement of surface area, volume and capacity of solid shapes."],"lo":["Determine the volume and capacity of solid shapes and solve problems that involve SI and imperial units in surface area, volume and capacity measurements."],"indicators":["Solve problems that involve SI and imperial units in volume/capacity measurements."],"focal":["Measurements of volume and capacity"],"exemplars":["Collaborative learning: Learners discuss and solve problems that involve the volume of 3-D objects and composite 3-D objects using formulas. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w20">{"year":2,"week":20,"id":"y2w20","title":"Volume and Capacity in the Real World","subtitle":"A step-by-step method for real problems; mixed SI and imperial units; filling times and flow rates; costs per cubic metre or cubic yard; water use and bills; measuring volume by displacement; how volume changes when every length is scaled; and design problems with containers, pools, tanks and packaging.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":7,"name":"Surface Areas and Volumes","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":18,"to":20},"outcomes":["Follow a clear method to model and solve real problems on volume and capacity.","Convert units within and between the SI and imperial systems while solving problems.","Use rates to find filling times, and costs from volumes.","Find the volume of an irregular object by displacement.","Use the volume scale factor $k^3$ for similar containers and judge whether answers are sensible."],"keywords":["model","volume","capacity","flow rate","filling time","cubic yard","gallon","litre","cost per unit","displacement","irregular solid","scale factor","similar containers","trapezoidal prism","rainwater harvesting","estimate","reasonableness"],"notes":[{"title":"A method for real problems","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Seven steps","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["**Understand** what is asked; sketch the object and identify its shape.","**Choose the formula**, or split the object into simple solids.","**Convert units** so that every measurement uses the same unit.","**Substitute** the values.","**Calculate** carefully (a calculator helps).","**Interpret** the result: litres? cost? time? Round sensibly (you cannot buy 4.3 bags).","**Check:** estimate, look at the units, and ask whether the answer is reasonable."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Useful facts","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Fact","Value"],"rows":[["1 m³","1000 litres"],["1 litre","1000 cm³"],["1 ft","12 in, so 1 ft³ $=1728$ in³"],["1 yd","3 ft, so 1 yd³ $=27$ ft³"],["1 US gallon","3.785 litres"],["1 ft³ of water","about 7.5 US gallons"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Rates and time","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **flow rate** tells you how fast a container fills or empties, for example 20 litres per minute:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{time}=\\frac{\\text{volume}}{\\text{rate}}\\qquad\\text{cost}=\\text{volume}\\times\\text{price per unit volume}"},{"k":"p","text":"Keep the units matching: if the rate is in litres per minute, the volume must be in litres."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Volume by displacement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An object sunk in water pushes aside (**displaces**) its own volume of water. The rise in water level in a container of known cross-section gives the volume of an irregular object such as a stone."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-displace","caption":"The rise in water level gives the stone's volume."}],"figs":["w20-displace"]},{"title":"Scaling","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If every length of a container is multiplied by $k$, its surface area is multiplied by $k^2$ and its **volume and capacity by $k^3$**."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-scale","caption":"Doubling every length multiplies the volume by 8."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Is it reasonable?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A bathtub holds a few hundred litres, a car's fuel tank about 40–70 litres, a classroom a few hundred cubic metres. If your answer is far from such sizes, check the units: a missing conversion (cm to m) is the most common error."}]}],"figs":["w20-scale"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Stacked books","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A book is 19 cm wide, 26 cm long and 2.5 cm thick. Eight such books are stacked. What volume do they take up?"}],"steps":["One book: $19\\times26\\times2.5=1235$ cm³.","Eight books: $8\\times1235=9880$ cm³ (about 9.9 litres of space)."],"answer":"9880 cm³","figs":[]},{"title":"Concrete for a pedestal","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A statue stands on a concrete block 9 ft long, 9 ft wide and 6 in high. Concrete costs GH₵70 per cubic yard. Find the cost of the concrete."}],"steps":["Same units: 6 in $=0.5$ ft.","$V=9\\times9\\times0.5=40.5$ ft³.","1 yd³ $=27$ ft³, so $V=\\dfrac{40.5}{27}=1.5$ yd³.","Cost $=1.5\\times70=$ GH₵105."],"answer":"GH₵105","figs":[]},{"title":"Water for showers","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Water costs GH₵1.50 per 1000 gallons. A family takes 4 showers a day, each lasting 10 minutes, and a shower delivers 2.5 gallons a minute. Find the monthly (30-day) cost of shower water, and the amount in litres."}],"steps":["Per day: $4\\times10\\times2.5=100$ gallons.","Per month: $30\\times100=3000$ gallons.","Cost $=\\dfrac{3000}{1000}\\times1.50=$ GH₵4.50.","In litres: $3000\\times3.785\\approx11\\,356$ L."],"answer":"GH₵4.50; about 11 356 litres","figs":[]},{"title":"A pool with a sloping floor","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A pool is 25 m long and 10 m wide. Its depth rises steadily from 1 m at one end to 3 m at the other. (a) How many litres does it hold? (b) How long would it take to fill at 250 litres per minute?"},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-pool","caption":"The pool is a prism with a trapezium cross-section."}],"steps":["(a) Cross-section (trapezium): $\\tfrac12(1+3)\\times25=50$ m².","Volume $=50\\times10=500$ m³ $=500\\,000$ litres.","(b) Time $=\\dfrac{500\\,000}{250}=2000$ min $=33$ h 20 min."],"answer":"(a) 500 000 L (b) 33 hours 20 minutes","figs":["w20-pool"]},{"title":"Filling a water tank","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A cylindrical water tank has radius 0.9 m and height 1.6 m. (a) Find its capacity in litres. (b) How long does a 20 L/min pipe take to fill it? (c) How many days does a full tank last a family using 150 L a day?"},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-tank","caption":"A cylindrical tank filled by a pipe."}],"steps":["(a) $V=\\pi(0.9)^2(1.6)\\approx4.07$ m³ $\\approx4072$ L.","(b) $\\dfrac{4072}{20}\\approx204$ min, about 3 h 24 min.","(c) $\\dfrac{4072}{150}\\approx27.1$, so it lasts **27** full days."],"answer":"(a) about 4072 L (b) about 3 h 24 min (c) 27 days","figs":["w20-tank"]},{"title":"Volume by displacement","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A stone is lowered into a cylindrical jar of radius 5 cm and the water level rises by 2 cm. Find the volume of the stone."}],"steps":["The stone displaces a cylinder of water of radius 5 cm and height 2 cm (see the figure in the notes).","$V=\\pi(5^2)(2)=50\\pi\\approx157$ cm³."],"answer":"about 157 cm³","figs":[]},{"title":"Scaling containers","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) An aquarium 12 in by 8 in by 8 in safely holds 6 guppies. How many could live in one 24 in by 16 in by 16 in, if the number depends on the volume? (b) A can 4 in tall with radius 1.5 in holds 10 pesewas' worth of drink. What is the drink in a can 8 in tall with radius 3 in worth?"}],"steps":["(a) Every length is doubled, so the volume is multiplied by $2^3=8$: $\\ 6\\times8=48$ guppies.","Check: $\\dfrac{24\\times16\\times16}{12\\times8\\times8}=\\dfrac{6144}{768}=8$ ✓.","(b) Again every length is doubled, so the volume is 8 times as big: $8\\times10=80$ pesewas."],"answer":"(a) 48 guppies (b) 80 pesewas","figs":[]},{"title":"A triangular prism goal","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A homemade soccer goal is a triangular prism. Its ends are right triangles with legs 4 ft and 8 ft, and the goal is 24 ft wide. How much space does it enclose, in ft³ and m³?"},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-goal","caption":"The goal is a triangular prism."}],"steps":["Area of each triangular end $=\\tfrac12\\times4\\times8=16$ ft².","Volume $=16\\times24=384$ ft³.","In m³: $384\\times0.0283168\\approx10.9$ m³."],"answer":"384 ft³, about 10.9 m³","figs":["w20-goal"]},{"title":"Is there enough sand?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A cylindrical sandbox has a diameter of 3 ft and is 10 in deep. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w21">{"year":2,"week":21,"id":"y2w21","title":"Data Project: Collection, Analysis and Interpretation","subtitle":"Planning and carrying out a mini-project on a real issue in the school or community; writing a project plan; collecting and organising data in a spreadsheet; summarising by group with averages, percentages and two-way tables; scatter graphs and correlation; drawing careful conclusions and recommendations; and presenting and publishing a report.","family":"data","section":{"no":8,"name":"Working with Data and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":21,"to":22},"outcomes":["Write a project plan with a clear question, method, instrument, sample, ethics and timeline.","Organise collected data in a table or spreadsheet and summarise it by group.","Use averages, percentages, two-way tables, charts and scatter graphs to analyse data.","Draw conclusions and recommendations, and state the limitations of the study.","Present and publish findings in a report, slides or an infographic."],"keywords":["project","research question","hypothesis","population","sample","instrument","pilot","consent","timeline","spreadsheet","AVERAGEIF","COUNTIF","two-way table","scatter graph","correlation","line of best fit","conclusion","recommendation","limitation","infographic","report"],"notes":[{"title":"Why do a data project?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Real problems in our schools and communities, such as health, sanitation, unemployment or poor results, need **evidence**. A few complaints are not enough: data from enough people shows whether a problem is real, how big it is and who is most affected. National bodies such as the Ghana Statistical Service collect data on malaria, population and living standards so that money and services go where they are most needed."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-stages","caption":"The eight stages of a mini data project."}],"figs":["w21-stages"]},{"title":"Writing a project plan","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"A project plan answers","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Topic and aim:** what issue, and why does it matter?","**Research question(s):** for example \"Is there a link between study time and maths grades?\" You may state a **hypothesis**: \"Students who study more get better grades.\"","**Population and sample:** who the question is about, and who you will actually ask (aim for 20–50 people; choose them fairly, Week 9).","**Method and instrument:** questionnaire, interview guide or observation guide, piloted first.","**Ethics:** consent, anonymity, honesty and respect for culture.","**Timeline and budget:** when each stage happens and what it costs."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Organising the data","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Enter every response as one **row** of a spreadsheet, with one **column** per question. Spreadsheet functions summarise the data quickly:"},{"k":"ul","items":["`=AVERAGE(D2:D31)` finds the mean of a column.","`=AVERAGEIF(B2:B31,\"Female\",D2:D31)` finds the mean for one group only.","`=COUNTIF(H2:H31,\"A\")` counts how many A grades there are.","`=COUNTIFS(B2:B31,\"Male\",H2:H31,\"A\")` counts males with grade A.","`=MEDIAN(D2:D31)` and `=STDEV.P(D2:D31)` give the median and standard deviation.","`=CORREL(D2:D31,I2:I31)` measures the strength of a linear relationship (from $-1$ to $1$)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Analysing and comparing groups","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Averages and spread** for each group (Week 11).","**Percentages** to compare groups of different sizes.","**Two-way tables** to count two features at once, such as gender and grade.","**Charts:** bar charts to compare groups, pie or waffle charts for parts of a whole (Week 10)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Scatter graphs and correlation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **scatter graph** plots two numerical variables for each person. If the points rise from left to right there is a **positive correlation**; if they fall, a **negative correlation**; if there is no pattern, **no correlation**. A **line of best fit** passes through the **mean point** $(\\bar x,\\bar y)$ and follows the trend."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Correlation is not causation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A link between two variables does not prove that one causes the other. Students who study more might also have more support at home. Also, do not use a line of best fit far outside the range of the data (extrapolation)."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Conclusions, limitations and recommendations","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A **conclusion** answers the research question using the evidence, with numbers.","**Limitations** are honest weaknesses: a small or unrepresentative sample, self-reported answers, a short time period.","**Recommendations** say what should be done, by whom, based on the findings."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Presenting and publishing","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A good **report** has a title, introduction (aim and question), method, results (tables and charts), discussion (conclusions and limitations), recommendations and an appendix (the instrument). Findings can also be shared as **slides**, an **infographic** (key numbers and simple charts on one page), or published in a school magazine, a newspaper such as the *Junior Graphic*, on local radio or on social media, always protecting the privacy of the people who took part."}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"A project plan","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write an outline plan for a project on \"Why do some students arrive late to school?\""}],"steps":["**Aim:** to find the main causes of lateness and suggest solutions.","**Questions:** How far do late students travel? What transport do they use? What time do they leave home?","**Sample:** 40 students, 10 from each form level, chosen at random from the register; plus 3 teachers on duty.","**Instrument:** a short anonymous questionnaire (piloted with 5 students) and an observation tally at the gate for one week.","**Ethics and timeline:** explain the purpose, ask for consent, no names; week 1 design and pilot, week 2 collect, week 3 analyse and report."],"answer":"Aim, questions, sample, instrument, ethics and timeline stated","figs":[]},{"title":"Averages by group","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Ten students reported their weekly study hours: males 5, 3, 2, 6, 4; females 10, 8, 7, 9, 5. Describe the relationship."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-scatter","caption":"Study hours against self-assessment."}],"steps":["The points rise from left to right: a **positive correlation**. (The spreadsheet gives `=CORREL(...)`$\\approx0.90$, a strong link.)","Mean point: $\\bar x=\\tfrac{59}{10}=5.9$, $\\ \\bar y=\\tfrac{73}{10}=7.3$; the line of best fit passes through $(5.9,\\,7.3)$.","Students who study more tend to rate their understanding higher, but this does not prove that studying causes the higher rating."],"answer":"Strong positive correlation; mean point $(5.9,\\,7.3)$","figs":["w21-scatter"]},{"title":"Interpreting a published table","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The table shows the number of children aged 6–59 months **tested** for malaria by rapid diagnostic test in a 2019 survey (Sept–Nov, total 2843). Interpret the data, and explain what you would need before concluding which region has the **most malaria**."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-malaria","caption":"Children tested for malaria by region, 2019."}],"steps":["Northern had the most children tested, $\\tfrac{509}{2843}\\approx17.9\\%$ of the total; Greater Accra the fewest, about 6.5%.","October accounts for $\\tfrac{1546}{2843}\\approx54\\%$ of all tests.","But the table counts children **tested**, not children found **positive**. To compare malaria levels, we need the number who tested positive in each region, as a **percentage of those tested** (the positivity rate).","A large count may simply mean a larger sample, so always read the title of a table carefully."],"answer":"Northern tested most (17.9%); positivity rates are needed to compare malaria levels","figs":["w21-malaria"]},{"title":"Conclusions and limitations","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write a conclusion, two limitations and two recommendations for the study-habits survey of 10 students."}],"steps":["**Conclusion:** in this sample, students who studied more hours reported higher understanding (strong positive correlation), and the females studied about twice as long as the males and obtained more A grades.","**Limitations:** only 10 students, not chosen at random; Design the data collection for a project on residents' awareness and practices, and explain how you would analyse it.","steps":["**Questionnaire** for about 50 households (one adult each, chosen systematically along each street): how waste is stored and disposed of, how often it is collected, whether they separate plastics, whether they know of recycling points.","**Observation guide:** count open dumps, blocked gutters and burning sites on each street over one week.","**Analysis:** percentages for each disposal method (waffle or bar chart), a two-way table of awareness against practice, and a map or table of observed dump sites. Conclusions should be linked to the evidence, for example \"65% burn plastic waste because there is no collection\"."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Explain why the conclusion \"Northern Region has the most malaria\" cannot be drawn from a table of the number of children tested in each region. What extra data are needed?","steps":["The table counts children **tested**, which depends on how many children were sampled in each region, not on how many were infected. A region with more children tested will show a larger number even if malaria is less common there.","To compare malaria levels we need the number of children who tested **positive** in each region, and the **positivity rate** $=\\dfrac{\\text{positive}}{\\text{tested}}\\times100\\%$. To compare burden we would also need each region's population of young children."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A student finds a strong positive correlation between the number of hours students spend on social media and the number of friends they report. She concludes that \"using social media makes you more popular\". Criticise this conclusion and suggest a better one.","steps":["Correlation shows only that the two variables tend to rise together. The cause could run the other way (students with many friends spend more time chatting online), or a third factor could affect both (for example owning a smartphone). The data are also self-reported, and \"number of friends\" is hard to measure.","A better conclusion: \"In this sample, students who spent more time on social media tended to report more friends. Further study is needed to find out why.\""],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"List the sections of a good project report and say what each should contain.","steps":["**Title** that states the people or organisations.","**Appendix:** a copy of the instrument and the raw data (without names)."],"answer":"","model":null}],"checklist":["I can write a project plan with a clear question, sample,
